blocks.text: You are familiar with the five kingdoms of living organisms. There are also creatures that do not possess a cellular organisation yet show some characteristics of living things. Viruses are the representatives of such organisms.

Viruses are extremely small infectious agents that can be seen only under the electron microscope. They range in size from 20 nm (parvovirus) to 250 nm (pox viruses), 10 to 1000 times smaller than most bacteria, which is why they pass through the pores of filter paper.

The central core of a virus is its genome, made of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. The core is surrounded by a protein coat called the capsid, which gives the virus its definite shape. The capsid is made of protein subunits called capsomeres; the number and kind of capsomeres is characteristic of a particular virus. The core and the capsid together are called the nucleocapsid.

In some animal viruses only, the nucleocapsid is covered by another membrane called the envelope. The envelope is a lipid-rich membrane derived from the host cell. Viruses without an envelope are called naked viruses.

blocks.title: Counting capsomeres
blocks.text: Herpes virus, which causes cold sores and chickenpox, contains 162 capsomeres in its capsid. Adenovirus, which causes the common cold, contains 252.

There is great diversity in the general appearance of viruses. Animal and plant viruses may be polyhedral (having many sides) or helical. Bacterial viruses, the bacteriophages, may be cubical, icosahedral (having 20 faces), helical or complex, with a polyhedral head and a rod-shaped tail.

blocks.alt: Seven virus forms, unlabelled: a polyhedral capsid with knobbed fibres at its corners, four spherical viruses covered with different spikes (knobbed, club-shaped or rod-like), a long wavy filamentous virus and a bacteriophage with a polyhedral head, a tail and tail fibres.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.10: Diversity in viruses' shapes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.10).

blocks.text: Bacteriophages are a diverse group of viruses that attack bacteria. They are among the most complex viruses. The best-known phages of Escherichia coli are the T-phages, of which there are many varieties. A T4 phage consists of a head and a tail. The head is an elongated pyramidal (two triangles with a common base), hexagonal (six-sided), prism-shaped structure. Its capsid is made of proteins, and its core contains a long double-stranded DNA. A straight tail is attached to the head. The tail has an inner core and an outer sheath, made of different proteins. A neck attaches the sheath to the head, and an end plate is present at the other end of the sheath. Six tail fibres are attached to the end plate; they help the phage attach to the bacterial wall. All of these structures are made of proteins.

blocks.alt: A T4 phage. The head is an elongated six-sided prism with pointed ends: its protein capsid holds the coiled core (DNA). A short neck joins the head to the tail, which is a ringed sheath around a central tail core. An end plate at the bottom carries six jointed tail fibres. Labels: Capsid, Core (DNA), Head, Neck, Sheath, Tail core, Tail, Tail fibres, End plate.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.11: Structure of a bacteriophage (T4 phage) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.11).

blocks.title: Phages as carriers
blocks.text: Bacteriophages are used as carriers in genetic engineering. The gene of interest is inserted into the DNA of a bacteriophage, which carries it into the target bacterial cell. When the virus incorporates its DNA into the bacterial chromosome, the gene of interest also becomes part of the bacterial DNA. Such transgenic bacteria (bacteria whose genome has DNA of some other organism) can be grown to get copies of the gene and the required protein.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) belongs to the retroviruses, a special group of animal viruses. Retroviruses contain RNA inside their capsid, and these structures are surrounded by a lipid-rich envelope. The envelope carries glycoprotein spikes, which help the virus identify and bind to its target. Retroviruses are spherical, about 100 nm in diameter. Their most distinguishing character is a specific enzyme, reverse transcriptase, which catalyses reverse transcription: a single-stranded RNA is reversely transcribed into a strand of DNA, and the enzyme then uses that DNA strand to complete a double helix of DNA.

blocks.alt: A round HIV particle in section. Knobbed glycoprotein spikes stand on the outer viral envelope; inside is an oval capsid holding two RNA strands and small reverse transcriptase molecules. Labels: Glycoprotein, Viral envelope, Capsid, RNA, Reverse transcriptase.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.12: Structure of HIV (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.12).

blocks.text: HIV is responsible for the disease AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). AIDS weakens the immune system of the patient. The disease is fatal because no one can survive without an immune system to defend against other viral and bacterial infections. The disease was first reported in 1981, and the first patients were homosexual; later, AIDS was found in non-homosexual patients too, who had received blood or blood products from AIDS patients. In 1984 it was discovered that the agent causing AIDS was a virus, and in 1986 the virus was named Human Immunodeficiency Virus. HIV is host-specific: it can multiply in monkeys but does not cause AIDS in them.

blocks.title: Where HIV came from
blocks.text: Experts have concluded that HIV originated in the jungles of Africa among wild chimps. Evidence suggests that a form of this virus entered the human species and became HIV by way of monkey bites or the ingestion of monkey meat and brains.
